parts.label: i
parts.text:
(i) Simplify
$$\sqrt{48}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}$$
Write your answer in the form $a\sqrt{3}$, where $a$ is an integer to be found.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Way 1: M1: Writes one of the terms of the given expression correctly in terms of $\sqrt{3}$, e.g. $\sqrt{48}=\sqrt{16}\sqrt{3}$ or $\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{3}$. A1: A correct answer of $2\sqrt{3}$ (correct answer with no working implies both marks). Way 2: M1: writes one of the terms correctly in terms of $\sqrt{12}$, e.g. $\sqrt{48}=2\sqrt{12}$ or $\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{12}$. A1: $2\sqrt{12}-\sqrt{12}=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}$. Way 3: M1: Writes $\sqrt{48}$ correctly as $\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{144}}{\sqrt{3}}$. A1: $\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=2\sqrt{3}$. Way 4: M1: Writes $\sqrt{48}$ correctly as $\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{144}}{\sqrt{3}}$, using $\sqrt{48}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{48}-...}{\sqrt{3}}$. A1: $\frac{12-6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=2\sqrt{3}$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Way 4: $\sqrt{48}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{48}-...}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{12-...}{\sqrt{3}}$ or $\sqrt{48}-\frac{6}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{48}-...}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{144}-...}{\sqrt{3}}$ M1

parts.label: ii
parts.text:
(ii) Solve the equation
$$3^{6x-3}=81$$
Write your answer as a rational number.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: Way 1: B1: For $81=3^4$ or $\log_3 81=6x-3$ (may be implied by subsequent work). M1: Solves an equation of the form $6x-3=k$ where $k$ is their power of 3. A1: $x=\frac{4+3}{6}=\frac{7}{6}$ or $1\frac{1}{6}$ or 1.16 with a dot over the 6. Way 2: B1: For $3=81^{1/4}$. M1: $81^{(6x-3)/4}=81\Rightarrow\frac{6x-3}{4}=1\Rightarrow x=...$ (equation of form $k(6x-3)=1$ where $k$ is their power of 81). A1: as above. Way 3: B1: For $81=9^2$ and $3=9^{1/2}$. M1: $9^{(6x-3)/2}=9^2\Rightarrow\frac{6x-3}{2}=2\Rightarrow x=...$ (equation of form $p(6x-3)=q$). A1: as above. Way 4: B1: For writing $3^{6x-3}$ correctly in terms of $3^{6x}$. M1: $3^{6x}=81\times3^3=3^7\Rightarrow 6x=7\Rightarrow x=...$ (equation of form $6x=k$ where $k$ is their $3^3\times81$ written as a power of 3). A1: $x=\frac{7}{6}$. Way 5: B1: Takes logs of both sides $\log 3^{6x-3}=\log 81$. M1: Solves $6x-3=\frac{\log 81}{\log 3}$ (equation of form $6x-3=k$ where $k$ is their $\frac{\log 81}{\log 3}$). A1: $6x-3=4\Rightarrow x=\frac{7}{6}$. Note: The question does not specify the form of the final answer and so if answers are left un-simplified as e.g. $\frac{\log_3 81+3}{6}$, $\frac{\log_3 2187}{6}$ then allow full marks if correct.

(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: For an attempt to complete the square $x^2-10x+23=(x\pm5)^2\pm A$. Note that if their $A=23$ then this is M0 by the General Principles. A1: Correct expression $(x-5)^2-2$. Ignore "=0".

questions.stem: Each year, Andy pays into a savings scheme. In year one he pays in £600. His payments increase by £120 each year so that he pays £720 in year two, £840 in year three and so on, so that his payments form an arithmetic sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find out how much Andy pays into the savings scheme in year ten.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: This mark is for $a+(n-1)d=600+9\times120$ or $600+8\times120$. A1: $=(£)1680$ with or without the "£". Answer only scores both marks. Listing: M1: Lists ten terms starting £600, £720, £840, £960, ... A1: Identifies the 10th term as $(£)1680$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Kim starts paying money into a different savings scheme at the same time as Andy. In year one she pays in £130. Her payments increase each year so that she pays £210 in year two, £290 in year three and so on, so that her payments form a different arithmetic sequence.
At the end of year $N$, Andy has paid, in total, twice as much money into his savings scheme as Kim has paid, in total, into her savings scheme.
(b) Find the value of $N$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme: Allow the use of $n$ instead of $N$ throughout in (b). B1: Identifies or uses $d=80$ for Kim. M1: Attempts a sum formula for Andy or Kim. A correct formula must be seen or implied with $a=600,d=120$ for Andy or $a=130,d=80$ for Kim. If B0 was scored, allow M1 here if Kim's incorrect "d" is used. A1: A correct equation in any form: $\frac{N}{2}\{2\times600+(N-1)\times120\}=2\times\frac{N}{2}\{2\times130+(N-1)\times80\}$. dM1: Proceeds to find a value for $N$ (allow if it leads to $N<0$), dependent on the first method mark and must be an equation that uses Andy's and Kim's sum: $20N=360\Rightarrow N=...$. A1: $(N=)18$. Ignore $N/n=0$ and if a correct value of $N$ is seen, isw any further reference to years etc. If you see $N=18$ with no working send Review. Listing approach: Year 1–18 totals for Andy: 600,1320,2160,3120,4200,5400,6720,8160,9720,11400,13200,15120,17160,19320,21600,24000,26520,29160. Kim: 130,340,630,1000,1450,1980,2590,3280,4050,4900,5830,6840,7930,9100,10350,11680,13090,14580. Kimx2: 260,680,1260,2000,2900,3960,5180,6560,8100,9800,11660,13680,15860,18200,20700,23360,26180,29160. B1: States or uses $d=80$ for Kim. M1: Attempts to find the total savings for Andy or Kim - must see the correct pattern for Andy (600,1320,2160,...) or Kim (130,340,630,...) (or Kimx2). A1: Correct totals for Andy and Kim (or Kimx2) at least as far as $n=18$. M1: Identifies when Andy's total = 2xKim's total. A1: $N=18$.

questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows the sketch of a curve with equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
The curve crosses the $y$-axis at $(0,4)$ and crosses the $x$-axis at $(5,0)$.
The curve has a single turning point, a maximum, at $(2,7)$.
The line with equation $y=1$ is the only asymptote to the curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State the coordinates of the turning point on the curve with equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x-2)$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Accept $(4,7)$ or $x=4,y=7$ or a sketch of $y=\mathrm{f}(x-2)$ with a maximum point marked at $(4,7)$. (Condone missing brackets.) There should be no other coordinates.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) State the solution of the equation $\mathrm{f}(2x)=0$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Allow $(x=)2.5$ or $(2.5,0)$ (condone missing brackets) but no other values or points. Allow a sketch of $\mathrm{f}(2x)$ with the only $x$-intercept marked at $x=2.5$ (allow $(0,2.5)$ marked in the correct place).

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) State the equation of the asymptote to the curve with equation $y=\mathrm{f}(-x)$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: $y=1$ (oe e.g. $y-1=0$). Must be an equation and not just '1' and no other asymptotes stated.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Given that the line with equation $y=k$, where $k$ is a constant, meets the curve $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$ at only one point,
(d) state the set of possible values for $k$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Either of $k\leqslant1$ or $k=7$. Accept either of $y\leqslant1$ or $y=7$. Note that $k=7$ may sometimes be seen embedded in e.g. $k=0,1,7$ and can score B1 here. B1: $k\leqslant1$ $k=7$. Both correct and in terms of $k$ with no other solutions.

questions.stem:
A sequence $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ is defined by
$$a_1=4$$
$$a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{a_n+1},\qquad n\geqslant1,n\in\mathbb{N}$$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the values of $a_2,a_3$ and $a_4$
Write your answers as simplified fractions.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Attempts to use the given recurrence relation correctly at least once e.g. $a_2=\frac{4}{4+1}$ or $a_3=\frac{\text{their }a_2}{(\text{their }a_2)+1}$ or $a_4=\frac{\text{their }a_3}{(\text{their }a_3)+1}$. May be implied by their term(s). A1: Two of $\frac{4}{5},\frac{4}{9},\frac{4}{13}$ which may be un-simplified. Accept for example $0.8,\frac{0.8}{1.8},...$ or $\frac{4}{5},\frac{4/5}{1+4/5},...$ A1: $\frac{4}{5},\frac{4}{9},\frac{4}{13}$ (Allow 0.8 for $\frac{4}{5}$).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that
$$a_n=\frac{4}{pn+q},\text{ where }p\text{ and }q\text{ are constants}$$
(b) state the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: $p=4$ or e.g. $a_n=\frac{4}{4n\pm...}$ OR uses 2 terms to set up and solve two correct equations for their fractions in $p$ and $q$ to obtain a value for $p$ or a value for $q$: $4=\frac{4}{p+q}$, $\frac{4}{5}=\frac{4}{2p+q}\Rightarrow p=...$ or $q=...$. A1: Either $a_n=\frac{4}{4n-3}$ OR $p=4$ and $q=-3$. Correct answer only scores both marks.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Hence calculate the value of $N$ such that $a_N=\dfrac{4}{321}$

questions.question_text:
A sequence $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ is defined by
$$a_1=4$$
$$a_{n+1}=\frac{a_n}{a_n+1},\qquad n\geqslant1,n\in\mathbb{N}$$
(a) Find the values of $a_2,a_3$ and $a_4$
Write your answers as simplified fractions.
(3)
Given that
$$a_n=\frac{4}{pn+q},\text{ where }p\text{ and }q\text{ are constants}$$
(b) state the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
(2)

(2)

The curve $C$ has equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$, where
$$\mathrm{f}'(x)=(x-3)(3x+5)$$

Follow through on incorrect indices but not for "+c". A1: All terms correct: $\mathrm{f}(x)=x^3-2x^2-15x+c$. Need not be simplified. A1: cao $(\mathrm{f}(x)=)x^3-2x^2-15x+36$ (all together and on one line).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Show that
$$\mathrm{f}(x)=(x-3)^2(x+A)$$
where $A$ is a constant to be found.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: Way 1: B1: $A=4$ correct value (may be implied). M1: Expands $(x-3)^2(x+A)=(x^2-6x+9)(x+A)=x^3+(A-6)x^2+(9-6A)x+9A$ and compares coefficients with their $\mathrm{f}(x)$ from part (a) to form 3 equations and attempts to solve at least two of them in an attempt to show that $A$ is the same in each case, or substitutes their $A$ to show that the coefficients are the same: $A-6=-2\Rightarrow A=4$; $9-6A=-15\Rightarrow A=4$; $9A=36\Rightarrow A=4$. A1: Fully correct proof - must use all 3 coefficients. Way 2: B1: $A=4$ (may be implied). M1: Expands $(x-3)^2(x+"4")$ fully in an attempt to show that the expansion gives the same expression found in part (a): $=(x-3)^2(x+4)=(x^2-6x+9)(x+4)=x^3-6x^2+4x^2+9x-24x+36=x^3-2x^2-15x+36$. A1: Fully correct proof (condone invisible brackets here e.g. around $x+4$ provided sufficient working is shown). Way 3: B1: $A=4$ (may be implied). M1: Divides their $\mathrm{f}(x)$ from part (a) by $(x-3)$ and divides their quotient by $(x-3)$ (allow $x^2\pm6x\pm9$) in an attempt to establish the value of $A$: $(x^3-2x^2-15x+36)\div(x-3)=x^2+x-12$; $(x^2+x-12)\div(x-3)=x+4$ or $(x^2+x-12)=(x+4)(x-3)$. A1: Fully correct proof. Note that this is also an acceptable proof: $A=4$ (may be implied); $x^3-2x^2-15x+36=(x-3)(x^2+x-12)=(x-3)(x-3)(x+4)=(x-3)^2(x+4)$.
